segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Let's design a video platform, covering upload, processing and playback at large scale.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: I would split it into three fairly independent systems. Ingestion, the transcoding pipeline, and the delivery path.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Starting with upload, large files over unreliable networks mean we need resumable, chunked uploads.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: The client requests an upload session, splits the file into parts, uploads each part independently and retries only the failed parts.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Direct to storage upload with a pre signed URL keeps the file bytes out of our application servers entirely.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: That is important. Proxying multi gigabyte files through application nodes wastes bandwidth and ties up connections for a long time.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Once all parts land, storage assembles the object and we emit an event that kicks off processing.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: The processing pipeline is where most of the complexity lives. We need multiple renditions at different resolutions and bitrates.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Adaptive bitrate streaming requires a ladder, maybe two hundred forty p up to four K, each encoded at an appropriate bitrate.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: And each rendition is segmented into short chunks, typically two to six seconds, with a manifest listing the available variants.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: The player then switches between renditions mid stream based on measured throughput and buffer level.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: That switching only works if the segments are aligned across renditions, with keyframes at identical timestamps.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Exactly. Misaligned keyframes cause visible glitches or failed switches, so the encoder must be configured with a fixed keyframe interval.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: For the transcoding itself, we should parallelize by splitting the source into segments and encoding them independently.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: That turns a long serial job into a wide parallel one, so a two hour film can be processed in minutes given enough workers.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: We need a job orchestrator with a directed graph of tasks, since thumbnail extraction, audio processing and each rendition can run concurrently.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Retries need to be idempotent at the segment level, so a failed worker just means that one segment is re encoded.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: We should also prioritize. A short clip from a popular creator should not sit behind a four hour upload in the same queue.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Multiple queues by expected duration and account tier solves most of that, plus a separate lane for reprocessing jobs.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Cost control matters enormously here, because transcoding is compute heavy and it is usually the largest line item.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: So we should encode the full ladder lazily for unpopular content, generating only the most common rendition up front.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Then if a video gains traction we backfill the remaining renditions on demand, which avoids paying for content nobody watches.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Spot or preemptible instances also fit this workload well, since segment level retries make interruption cheap.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Let's move to delivery. The content delivery network does the heavy lifting, serving segments from edge locations near the viewer.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Our origin only sees cache misses, so the origin fleet can be small relative to the total delivered bandwidth.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Cache hit ratio is the metric to obsess over. A few percentage points of miss rate translate into large origin costs.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Segment URLs should be stable and immutable, which makes them perfectly cacheable with a very long time to live.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Manifests are different. For live content the manifest updates constantly and needs a very short cache lifetime.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: That split, immutable segments and volatile manifests, is the core caching insight for streaming.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: For access control, we use signed URLs with short expiry so a leaked link stops working quickly.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: And for premium content, digital rights management with license servers, though that adds significant client complexity.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: We should also think about pre positioning. For a highly anticipated release we can push content to edges before launch.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Otherwise the first wave of viewers all miss cache simultaneously and hammer the origin at exactly the worst moment.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Let's talk about live streaming, which changes several assumptions.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: The ingest is a continuous stream rather than a file, using a protocol like RTMP or a low latency variant.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Transcoding must happen in real time, so we cannot parallelize by splitting the file. We parallelize across renditions instead.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: And latency becomes a first class requirement. Standard segmented streaming adds ten to thirty seconds of delay.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Low latency modes use shorter segments and chunked transfer, pushing partial segments before they are complete.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: That cuts latency to a few seconds, at the cost of less efficient caching and more requests per viewer.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: We also need a failover path for the ingest, because a dropped encoder connection means dead air for every viewer.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Dual ingest from the broadcaster into two regions, with automatic switchover, is the standard answer for important events.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: On the playback side, we need client telemetry to understand real quality, not just server side metrics.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Startup time, rebuffer ratio, average bitrate and playback failures are the four numbers that actually describe the experience.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: Rebuffer ratio is the one users feel most. A slightly lower bitrate is almost always better than a stall.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: The player's adaptation algorithm should therefore be conservative on the way up and aggressive on the way down.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: For storage, we keep the original master for reprocessing, plus all the renditions, which multiplies the footprint significantly.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: We should tier that storage. Masters go to cold archival storage, and unpopular renditions can be deleted and regenerated if needed.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: To summarize, resumable direct to storage uploads, segment parallel transcoding with lazy ladder generation, and edge delivery with immutable segments.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Plus signed access, pre positioning for launches, a separate real time path for live, and client side quality telemetry.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_01
segments.text: The economics drive most decisions here. Transcoding compute and egress bandwidth dominate, so the architecture follows the cost.
